prompt: When a valve is opened between a gas and an evacuated chamber, the gas spontaneously fills the chamber. According to the section, what do the state functions U and H tell us about whether this will happen?

choices.text: Nothing about which way it will go
It happens because U decreases as the gas expands
choices.why: When an ideal gas expands into vacuum, U doesn't change at all. The section's point is that U and H give no clue about the direction.

choices.text: It happens because H increases as the gas expands
choices.why: H gives no more guidance than U here. Neither energy function tells us which way the process will go.

choices.text: It happens only because the gas gives off heat
choices.why: No heat flows when a gas expands into vacuum. Whether a process is spontaneous is decided by something other than energy or heat.

explanation: A gas fills an evacuated chamber, and two separated gases mix, without U or H pointing the way. Energy alone does not decide whether a process is spontaneous.

prompt: KNO3 dissolves in water on its own, and the solution gets cold. What does this show?

choices.text: It is spontaneous even though it takes in heat
KNO3 must not really dissolve spontaneously
choices.why: It does dissolve on its own; the section uses it as an example of a spontaneous process. It shows that taking in heat doesn't stop a process from happening.

choices.text: Only processes that give off heat are spontaneous
choices.why: This is the very idea the example disproves. Dissolving KNO3 is spontaneous, yet the solution cools.

choices.text: Dissolving KNO3 breaks the first law
choices.why: Energy is still conserved; the heat comes from the solution, which cools. The example shows that the first law alone can't predict spontaneity.

explanation: The cooling shows that dissolving KNO3 takes in heat, yet it happens spontaneously. Dissolving KOH, which warms the solution, is spontaneous too, so giving off heat is not what makes a process go.

prompt: The first law, ΔU = q + w, says that energy is conserved. Why does the section say it is not enough to describe nature?

choices.text: It can't say which way a process will go
It holds only for ideal gases, not for solutions
choices.why: The first law holds for every system, solutions included. The trouble is that it says nothing about the direction of a process.

choices.text: It breaks down for processes that take in heat
choices.why: Energy is conserved when KNO3 dissolves and takes in heat, too. The first law holds; it just can't tell which processes are spontaneous.

choices.text: It leaves out the work done on the system
choices.why: Work is right there in ΔU = q + w. What the first law lacks is any way to tell which direction a process will take.

explanation: Energy is conserved whether KNO3 dissolves (and cools the solution) or KOH dissolves (and warms it). Both are spontaneous, so the first law alone can't predict which way a process goes.

prompt: The section lists what the new state function entropy has achieved so far. For which systems does it already give a criterion for spontaneity?

choices.text: Isolated systems only
All systems, open or closed
choices.why: A criterion for all systems is still on the section's wish list. So far, entropy decides spontaneity only for isolated systems.

choices.text: Only systems at constant pressure
choices.why: Constant pressure isn't the condition the section names. The criterion it has so far works for isolated systems.

choices.text: No systems yet
choices.why: The section says we already have a criterion. Its limit is that it works only for isolated systems.

explanation: Entropy gives a spontaneity criterion for isolated systems. Extending it to all systems, not just isolated ones, is one of the two items left on the wish list.

prompt: Besides a spontaneity criterion for all systems, what is the other problem the section says remains open?

choices.text: What the state function S actually is
How to measure the heat q in a process
choices.why: Measuring heat is not the open problem. The section asks what S really is, which leads it to the molecular level.

choices.text: Whether energy is conserved in every process
choices.why: The first law already settles that energy is conserved. The open question is what the new state function S is.

choices.text: Why work can be turned fully into heat
choices.why: Turning work into heat is the easy direction and is not the open question. The remaining problem is what S is.

explanation: We have a new state function S but don't yet know what it is. To understand it better, the section turns to what happens at the molecular level.

prompt: Work and heat are both forms of energy, but converting one into the other is easier in one direction. Which conversion does entropy let us predict limits on?

choices.text: Heat into work, as in power generation
Work into heat, as in dissipation
choices.why: Turning work into heat (dissipation) is the easy direction. The limits apply to turning heat into work.

choices.text: Neither; both directions are equally easy
choices.why: The section stresses an asymmetry: one direction is easier than the other. Heat into work is the limited one.

choices.text: Both directions are impossible
choices.why: Both conversions happen all the time: friction turns work into heat, and engines turn heat into work. Only heat into work is limited.

explanation: Work turns into heat easily (dissipation), but turning heat into work (power generation) is limited. Entropy lets us predict those limits.

prompt: The section says entropy has so far been introduced as a phenomenological theory. What does that mean?

choices.text: S came from observed behavior, not a molecular model
S can be measured directly with a special instrument
choices.why: No instrument reads S directly. Phenomenological means S was introduced from observed behavior, without explaining it at the molecular level.

choices.text: S was later shown by experiments to be wrong
choices.why: The section says there is nothing scientifically wrong with a phenomenological theory. It just doesn't yet explain S in molecular terms.

choices.text: S was derived from the motions of single molecules
choices.why: That molecular picture is exactly what is still missing. A phenomenological theory describes the phenomenon without it.

explanation: A phenomenological theory introduces S as a phenomenon of its own, from observed behavior. Nothing is wrong with that, but understanding the molecular cause makes the theory more powerful.

prompt: To understand entropy better, where does the section say we need to look?

choices.text: At the molecular level, with statistics
At larger and larger macroscopic samples
choices.why: Larger samples only repeat the macroscopic picture. The section turns to the molecular level and statistics over many molecules.

choices.text: At the heat that each process releases
choices.why: Heat release doesn't decide spontaneity, as KNO3 shows. The section looks at molecules and counts how their energy is distributed.

choices.text: At the total energy of the system alone
choices.why: The total energy can stay the same while S changes. The section looks at the molecular level and counts the ways energy is distributed.

explanation: To understand entropy, the section leaves the macroscopic world and looks at what happens on a molecular level. Because there are so many molecules, it needs statistics, starting with counting arrangements.

prompt: Why can n distinguishable objects, such as playing cards, be arranged in n! different ways?

choices.text: The choices multiply: n, then n − 1, then n − 2, …
Any of the n objects can go first, giving n ways
choices.why: n counts only the choices for the first place. After that, n − 1 objects remain for the second place, and so on, so the total is n!.

choices.text: Each object can go in any of the n places on its own
choices.why: That would let two objects share a place and give n^(n) ways. Each place used up leaves one fewer choice, giving n(n − 1)(n − 2)… = n!.

choices.text: The choices add up: n + (n − 1) + … + 1
choices.why: The choices for successive places multiply, not add. The sum n + (n − 1) + … + 1 is much smaller than n!.

explanation: For the first place there are n choices, for the second n − 1 (one object is spoken for), and so on down to 1. Multiplying gives W = n(n − 1)(n − 2)… × 2 × 1 = n!.

prompt: In thermodynamics, what is the number of ways W of arranging a set of objects usually called?

choices.text: The number of realizations
The molecular partition function
choices.why: The partition function is a sum of Boltzmann factors, not a count of arrangements. W is called the number of realizations.

choices.text: The number of degrees of freedom
choices.why: Degrees of freedom count independent coordinates or motions. W, the count of arrangements, is the number of realizations.

choices.text: The heat capacity
choices.why: Heat capacity measures how energy changes with temperature. W counts arrangements and is called the number of realizations.

explanation: The section calls W the number of realizations: the number of distinct ways the same overall situation can be realized. Boltzmann later links it to entropy.

prompt: When n objects fall into groups whose members can't be told apart, why is n! divided by a! b! c! …, where a, b, c, … are the group sizes?

choices.text: Swapping within a group changes nothing
The groups must be kept in a fixed order
choices.why: Members of different groups can sit anywhere in the row. The division removes the swaps within each group, which don't produce a new arrangement.

choices.text: Each group then counts as a single object
choices.why: Each member still takes its own place in the row. Only the swaps among members of the same group are removed.

choices.text: Larger groups give more arrangements
choices.why: Larger groups give fewer distinct arrangements, since more swaps change nothing. That is why n! is divided by the factorials of the group sizes.

explanation: Swapping two identical members of a group gives the same arrangement, so n! overcounts. Dividing by a! b! c! … removes those swaps, giving W = (n!)/(a! b! c! …), with a + b + c + … = n.

prompt: Ensembles in thermodynamics hold about Avogadro's number of systems, so their factorials are horribly large and the section works with logarithms. Which expression is Stirling's approximation for ln N!?

choices.text: ln N! ≈ N ln N − N
ln N! ≈ N ln N + N
choices.why: The sign of the last term is wrong. Stirling's approximation is ln N! ≈ N ln N − N.

choices.text: ln N! ≈ ln N − N
choices.why: This is missing the factor N in front of ln N, which makes it far too small. Stirling's approximation is ln N! ≈ N ln N − N.

choices.text: ln N! ≈ N! ln N
choices.why: This still contains the huge factorial that the approximation is meant to remove. Stirling's approximation is ln N! ≈ N ln N − N.

explanation: Stirling's approximation, ln N! ≈ N ln N − N, replaces the logarithm of a huge factorial with simple terms. It works very well for the enormous numbers met in thermodynamics.

prompt: Since 1960, the number of breeding storks in Germany and the human birth rate there have followed almost the same curve, with a correlation above 0.98. What does this show?

choices.text: A correlation, not cause and effect
That storks really do bring babies
choices.why: A high correlation alone doesn't prove causality. Both curves follow a common underlying factor: the choices people made.

choices.text: That more babies attract more storks
choices.why: A correlation doesn't show causality in either direction. A common underlying factor drives both curves.

choices.text: That one of the data sets must be wrong
choices.why: The data can be fine and the correlation real. It just doesn't prove that one causes the other.

explanation: Two quantities can rise and fall together because of a common underlying factor. You can conclude causality only if you are sure no other factors intervene.

prompt: Why does the section call the expansion of an ideal gas into vacuum a wonderful model experiment?

choices.text: Only the expansion and an entropy change take place
It releases a large amount of heat that is easy to measure
choices.why: No heat flows when a gas expands into vacuum, and no work is done. Only the entropy changes, which makes the cause easy to trace.

choices.text: The gas does a lot of work on the vacuum
choices.why: There is nothing to push against in a vacuum, so no work is done. Only the entropy changes, which is what makes it a clean model.

choices.text: The energy of the gas drops sharply as it spreads out
choices.why: When an ideal gas expands into vacuum, its energy doesn't change at all. Only the entropy changes.

explanation: In this expansion there is no energy change, no heat, no work, no change in mass and no interactions. With only the entropy changing, the cause of that change can be traced at the atomic level.

prompt: When an ideal gas expands into vacuum, its internal energy U stays the same. According to the section, what does change at the molecular level?

choices.text: The energy states crowd closer together
The energy states spread farther apart
choices.why: The state energies, E_kin = (h^2)/(8ma^2) × (n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2), fall as the box side a grows. So the states move closer together, not farther apart.

choices.text: Each molecule ends up with less energy
choices.why: U and the average energy ⟨E⟩ stay the same. What changes is the spacing of the states, which shrinks as the box grows.

choices.text: The number of molecules in the box grows
choices.why: No mass enters or leaves the gas as it expands. What changes is the set of energy states, which crowd closer together.

explanation: A particle in a box of side a has energies E_kin = (h^2)/(8ma^2) × (n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2), so a bigger box makes the spacing between states smaller. The gas then has more states over which to spread its unchanged energy.

prompt: Why does the average energy ⟨E⟩ of the molecules stay the same when an ideal gas expands into vacuum?

choices.text: Because the internal energy U doesn't change
Because the energy states don't change
choices.why: The states do change: they move closer together as the box grows. ⟨E⟩ stays the same because U doesn't change.

choices.text: Because heat flows in to make up for the loss
choices.why: No heat flows in this expansion, and none is needed. U doesn't change, so ⟨E⟩ stays the same.

choices.text: Because the gas does work that cancels the loss
choices.why: Expanding against vacuum, the gas does no work. U simply doesn't change, and ⟨E⟩ is U shared out over the molecules.

explanation: In the expansion into vacuum there is no heat and no work, so U doesn't change. The average energy ⟨E⟩, taken over the many molecules of the gas, stays the same even though the states themselves shift.

prompt: The section follows just two particles, with equally spaced energy states, as a gas expands into vacuum. Their average energy ⟨E⟩ is the same before and after. What changes?

choices.text: There are more realizations of that same ⟨E⟩
The total energy of the two particles rises
choices.why: ⟨E⟩ and the total energy stay the same. What grows is the number of ways, W, of realizing that energy.

choices.text: There are fewer realizations, since the particles spread out
choices.why: More states become available as the box grows, so the number of realizations goes up, not down.

choices.text: Both particles must move to the lowest state
choices.why: Nothing forces them into the ground state, and that would lower ⟨E⟩. With more states available, there are more ways to realize the same ⟨E⟩.

explanation: Before the expansion the section counts three realizations, W_1, W_2 and W_3, with the same ⟨E⟩; after it, with more states available, there are more realizations in the same energy interval. The number of realizations grows while the energy stays put.

prompt: According to Boltzmann's postulate, what lies at the root of the entropy function?

choices.text: The number of ways to distribute the energy
The total energy that the system contains
choices.why: When a gas expands into vacuum, its total energy stays the same while S rises. Boltzmann tied S to the number of ways that energy can be distributed.

choices.text: The heat it has released to its surroundings
choices.why: Heat release doesn't decide spontaneity, and no heat flows when a gas expands into vacuum. S depends on the number of ways the energy can be distributed.

choices.text: The temperature of the system, and nothing else
choices.why: When an ideal gas expands into vacuum, its temperature doesn't change, yet S rises. S reflects the number of ways to distribute the energy.

explanation: Boltzmann postulated that entropy comes not from the total energy, which can stay the same, but from W, the number of ways that energy can be distributed over the ensemble. More ways means higher entropy.

prompt: All the realizations W counted by Boltzmann have the same total energy. What else, then, can W be called?

choices.text: The ensemble's degree of degeneracy, Ω
The partition function of the ensemble
choices.why: The partition function is a sum of Boltzmann factors over states of different energies. Realizations that share one energy count its degeneracy, Ω.

choices.text: The average energy ⟨E⟩ of the ensemble
choices.why: W is a pure count, not an energy. Since all the realizations share one energy, W is the degree of degeneracy, Ω.

choices.text: The number of members in the ensemble
choices.why: W counts ways of distributing the energy, which is a different number from the count of members. It is the ensemble's degeneracy, Ω.

explanation: States of the same energy are degenerate. Because every realization has the same total energy, the number of realizations W is the degree of degeneracy Ω of the ensemble.

prompt: Combining two ensembles multiplies their numbers of realizations, W_tot = W_1 × W_2, while their entropies should add. Why did Boltzmann therefore make S depend on the logarithm of W?

choices.text: A logarithm turns a product into a sum
A logarithm makes S grow faster than W
choices.why: A logarithm grows much more slowly than W. Boltzmann chose it because ln(W_1 × W_2) = ln W_1 + ln W_2, so entropies add.

choices.text: A logarithm turns a sum into a product
choices.why: It is the other way round: ln(W_1 × W_2) = ln W_1 + ln W_2. The product of W values becomes a sum of entropies.

choices.text: A logarithm keeps S below 1 for any W
choices.why: ln W can be very large when W is large. The logarithm was chosen because it turns the product W_1 × W_2 into a sum.

explanation: Since ln(W_1 × W_2) = ln W_1 + ln W_2, S = k_B ln W makes the entropy of the combined ensemble the sum of the two entropies. That is why Boltzmann wrote S = k_B ln W.

prompt: According to the section, why do two different gases mix spontaneously when the valve between them is opened?

choices.text: Each gas gets more energy states, so W and S increase
The mixture has a lower energy than the separate gases
choices.why: For ideal gases, mixing doesn't change the energy. The driving force is the rise in W, and so in S, as each gas gets more states to use.

choices.text: Heat flows in from the surroundings and pushes them together
choices.why: No heat is needed for ideal gases to mix. Each gas gains energy states in the larger volume, which raises W and S.

choices.text: The gas molecules attract each other strongly
choices.why: Ideal gas molecules don't interact. They mix because spreading through the whole volume gives more energy states, raising W and S.

explanation: In the larger volume each gas has more energy states to play with, which increases the number of realizations W. A larger W means a larger S, and that drives the spontaneous expansion or mixing.

prompt: n distinguishable objects can be arranged in a row in W = n! ways. In how many ways can six different playing cards be laid out in a row?
explanation: W = 6! = 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 720. There are 6 choices for the first card, 5 for the second, and so on down to 1 for the last.

prompt: Four coins, two identical pennies and two identical dimes, are laid out in a row. Using W = (n!)/(a! b!), where a and b are the sizes of the groups of identical coins, how many distinguishable arrangements are there?
explanation: W = (4!)/(2! 2!) = 24/(2 × 2) = 6: PPDD, PDPD, PDDP, DPPD, DPDP and DDPP. Without the division there would be 4! = 24 orders, but swapping identical coins doesn't give a new arrangement.

prompt: One ensemble can be realized in W_1 = 10 ways and a second in W_2 = 25 ways. Taken together, every realization of the first can be combined with every realization of the second, so W_tot = W_1 × W_2. What is W_tot?
explanation: W_tot = 10 × 25 = 250. The numbers of realizations multiply, so an additive entropy needs a logarithm: ln 250 = ln 10 + ln 25.

prompt: Two particles, 1 and 2, share a total energy of 2ε, and their states are equally spaced. Before an expansion the states lie at 0, ε, 2ε, …, which gives three realizations: (0, 2ε), (ε, ε) and (2ε, 0). After the expansion the spacing is halved, so the states lie at 0, ε/2, ε, 3ε/2, 2ε, …. How many realizations of the same total energy 2ε are there now?
explanation: Particle 1 can now have 0, ε/2, ε, 3ε/2 or 2ε, and particle 2 takes the rest, giving 5 realizations. The total energy is unchanged, but halving the spacing raised the number of realizations from 3 to 5.

prompt: An ensemble has A = 20 systems, all in the same state, so a_1 = 20 and every other a_j = 0. Using W = (A!)/(a_1! a_2! …) and 0! = 1, how many realizations W does this ensemble have?
explanation: W = (20!)/(20! × 0! × 0! × …) = 1. There is only one way to put every system in the same state, the very orderly case for which Boltzmann's S = k_B ln W is zero.
